_changelog: v1.1.0 (2026-10-14) plain-language pass: every technical word explained where it first appears; options in plain words
title: The Ring

post.author: u/winter_ledger_araminta
post.title: I keep the winter books at a pier fairground. The night watchman says the carousel never stops, and on Tuesday its ride log put more riders on one horse than the whole platform holds.

blocks.text: Gullsway Pier shuts its fairground from November to Easter. The carousel stands under tarpaulin at the end of the pier: eight wooden horses on a platform that holds 64 riders. I keep the winter books in the pass office beside it, at night, while the renewal letters print. On my first night Hamish, the watchman, nodded at the screen above my desk and said, "That one never stops."

He meant the Carousel, the system Cressida built in 2011 to keep our season passes. There are 12,000, and she calls each pass record a rider. They live on eight small servers, the computers that store and answer, named after the real horses. The ice rink's gates, open all winter, check every pass against them. The screen draws a ring of 360 degrees with each horse bolted at one place on it, a single degree. Seating a rider takes three steps. The pass number goes through a hash, a fixed recipe that turns it into the same point on the ring every time. From that point, the Carousel goes clockwise to the next horse. The rider sits on that horse, and a spare copy sits on the horse after it. All winter the drawing turns, slowly, as the letters read it.

At 03:00 it writes a ride log. The top line shows the time, the horses and the riders in all. Below it, each name is a horse, and the number beside it is how many riders that horse carries. Every night it says the same.

03:00  RIDE LOG   8 horses   12,000 riders
       Marigold  5,645     Dapple    1,414
       Tansy     1,352     Juniper   1,160
       Clover      932     Cobweb      776
       Saffron     721     Pewter        0

Pewter has carried nobody all winter. Juniper and Tansy are the sturdy ones, Cressida says, with twice the memory, the server's fast working space, of the rest. They carry a fraction of what old Marigold does. On Tuesday Dapple went off for repair: its disk, where it keeps records with the power off, had failed. The next log starts with a line saying when Dapple went off, then shows the same counts as before:

Tue 22:40  Dapple off for repair (disk)
03:00  RIDE LOG   7 horses   12,000 riders
       Marigold  7,059     Tansy     1,352
       Juniper   1,160     Clover      932
       Cobweb      776     Saffron     721
       Pewter        0
Seven thousand and fifty-nine riders on one wooden horse. The platform holds 64.

Marigold's fans ran all night, and on Wednesday the rink's gates took so long over each pass that people queued in the sleet. Dapple is back now. The spring pass sale opens in March, and Cressida wants a ninth horse, Nutmeg, before it. She says we can change anything except the passes.

Each arrow is labelled with the arc the next horse owns: 169, 33.5, 21.5, 0.01, 40.99, 24.5, 28.5 and 42 degrees. 12,000 riders, each on the next horse clockwise.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Read Cressida's screen before anyone sells you a fix. What she built is called a hash ring, or consistent hashing: the hash places each record on a circle, and each server owns a stretch of it. Each horse owns an arc: the stretch of ring from the horse before it, going clockwise, up to its own degree. Every pass hashed into that stretch rides that horse. A good hash scatters pass numbers evenly round the ring, like darts thrown blind at a clock face. That means a horse's riders follow the size of its arc. So measure them. Which arc is widest, and which is narrowest? When Dapple went off, how many horses shared its riders, and why that many? Now picture Nutmeg bolted at whatever degree its name hashes to: whose riders could it take, and how many horses would notice? Last, Juniper and Tansy have twice the memory. Where on that screen does the ring know it?

replies.author: u/winter_ledger_araminta
replies.text: Hamish lent me a protractor. Marigold's arc is 169 degrees, nearly half the ring. Pewter's is a hundredth of a degree. Cressida says she typed the degrees in by eye in 2011, where the wooden horses stand, and nobody has touched them since.

comments.author: u/divide_by_eight_bellamy
comments.text: It's a circle. Divide it by eight. Put a horse every 45 degrees and every arc is exactly an eighth of the ring, so every horse carries an eighth of the riders, give or take what the hash does. I did exactly that on our cache ring two years ago, the ring of servers that keep quick copies for our site, and the graphs have been flat as a millpond since. No new machinery, just eight numbers typed in again.

comments.author: u/mod_eight_dorcas
comments.text: Why a ring at all? Seat each rider by pass number mod 8, the remainder when you divide the number by 8. Your passes run from 1 to 12,000, so every horse gets exactly 1,500, not one rider more or less. You can't get flatter than that.

replies.author: u/winter_ledger_araminta
replies.text: Cressida says that's how passes were seated before 2011. She won't say why she stopped.

reply.prompt: Dapple is back. In March the spring sale opens and Nutmeg joins as a ninth horse. What should Cressida change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Re-space the eight horses by hand, one every 45 degrees, so every arc is the same size and each horse carries an eighth of all the riders.
options.verdict: Even today, uneven after any change
options.part2: Cressida typed in eight new degrees in February, 45 apart. The ride log flattened overnight: Pewter carried the most, 1,569, and Saffron the fewest, 1,417. Then Nutmeg arrived in March, and eight eighths no longer added up, so she re-spaced all nine, 40 degrees apart. 4,784 of 12,000 riders changed horse in one night, 39.9 percent, and every one of their records had to be copied to its new horse on the first night of the sale. In April Dapple went off for another disk. Nobody re-spaces for a two-day repair, so all 1,383 of its riders landed on Juniper, which carried 2,714.
options.senior: Even spacing fixes today's arcs by hand and says nothing about tomorrow's. With one place per horse, a horse that leaves still hands its whole arc to one neighbour. And keeping the spacing even after an addition means moving every horse, which moves far more riders than the newcomer takes: 4,784 here. A ring that leaves the old horses alone moves only the newcomer's share.

options.text: Give every horse many places on the ring, more for the sturdy ones, and put each rider's copies on the next different horses clockwise.
options.part2: Cressida gave every horse 128 places, each found by hashing the horse's name with a number, and Juniper and Tansy 256 each. Raising the places moved 10,351 riders once, and the sturdier horses' extra places 1,944 more, on two quiet nights in January. The next ride log was the flattest the Carousel has written: Juniper carried 2,487 of its fair 2,400, and the furthest from fair was Dapple, 1,353 against 1,200. She changed the copies too, to three steps: start from a rider's place, walk clockwise, and take the next horse that doesn't already hold a copy of that rider. With 128 places, the old walk would have put both copies of 1,439 riders on one horse. In March Dapple went off for another disk, and its 1,353 riders scattered over all seven others, 344 to Tansy at the most and 25 to Clover at the least. Nutmeg joined the week after and took 1,167 riders, 9.7 percent, a few from every horse.
options.senior: One random place per horse makes uneven arcs. Many places per horse average the luck out, so each horse's share comes close to fair, and a horse that leaves scatters its riders over every other horse instead of one. Places in proportion to capacity, how much a machine can carry, let a bigger machine carry more. A new horse takes only the riders it now owns, a little from everyone. And copies must walk to different machines, or two copies of a rider share one disk and die together. This is the design of Dynamo, Amazon's own database, and of Cassandra, a widely used free database, through its num_tokens setting.

options.text: Go back to seating riders by pass number mod 8: every horse gets exactly 1,500, and nobody has to judge where a horse is bolted ever again.
options.part2: Cressida switched the Carousel back to seating by pass number mod 8 in February, and the ride log was perfect: 1,500 on every horse. In March Nutmeg joined, and mod 8 became mod 9: 10,665 of 12,000 riders changed horse in one night, 88.9 percent, on the first night of the sale, and the rink's gates looked for most passes on a horse that didn't have them yet. In April Dapple went off for repair, and mod 9 became mod 8: 10,671 riders moved again. When Dapple came back two days later, they all moved back.
options.senior: A key is the value used to place a record, here the pass number, and a node is one server in the group. Mod spreads keys perfectly while the number of nodes holds still, and moves nearly every key when it changes, because a key's remainder depends on the count. The ring ties each key to a point that doesn't depend on how many nodes there are, so a change moves only the keys between the changed node and its neighbour. That is the reason consistent hashing exists. The ring's trouble is balance, and the fix for balance is more places per node, not a return to mod.

options.text: Leave the ring as it is, and make every horse strong enough for the busiest arc, so any horse could carry Marigold's whole crowd on its own.
options.part2: Cressida priced eight new servers, each with room for 7,059 riders, the most any horse has carried. That's room for 56,472 riders to hold 12,000, so nearly four fifths of it sits idle, and Pewter still carries nobody. It works: Dapple went off again in March, and Marigold carried 7,059 without a sound from her fans. Then Nutmeg joined at the one degree its name hashes to and took 691 riders, every one of them from Tansy. Cressida asked what happens if Marigold herself goes off: all 5,645 of her riders land on Juniper, 6,805 in all, inside the new size, just.
options.senior: Sizing every node, every server, for the worst arc is simple and it works. When machines are cheap next to engineers' time, it can be the right call for a while. But you pay for room that idles every night, the empty node stays empty, a removal still dumps a whole arc on one neighbour, and the next node added takes from one neighbour only. Many places per node get the same safety from the machines you already have.

sim.title: Run Cressida's ring
sim.lede: You're Cressida at the pass office screen. The ring runs once round, 360 degrees. Each of the 12,000 riders is a season pass: its number is hashed to a point on the ring, and it sits on the horse that owns the first place clockwise from that point. It opens as built, with each of the eight horses in one place, at the degrees in Araminta's sketch. Change the places per horse (each extra place is hashed from the horse's name and a number), give the sturdier horses, Juniper and Tansy, twice the places, add a horse (Nutmeg, then Quince), send one off for repair, change the number of riders, or seat them another way: every place hashed, evenly spaced by hand (adding a horse re-spaces them all, a repair leaves a gap), or pass number mod the number of horses. Each change logs how many riders changed horse and where they went. A horse's fair share is the riders divided among the horses running, counting a sturdier horse twice when it has twice the places; the busiest stat is the worst horse's riders divided by its fair share. Each rider's copies walk clockwise from its place, one per place; switch on skipping to pass over a horse that already holds one. Re-bolt at random draws new places from the sim's seeded random numbers.
sim.tryThis: Try this: as built, Marigold carries 5,645 and Pewter 0, 3.76 times a fair share. Send Dapple off for repair: all 1,414 of its riders land on Marigold, 7,059. Bring it back and raise the places per horse through 4, 16, 32 and 128: the busiest falls from 3.76 to 1.06. At 128, send Dapple off again: 1,540 riders scatter over all seven, 278 at most to one. Bring it back, set copies to 3: 3,571 riders have two copies on one horse. Switch on skipping: none. Now set four horses and add one: at 128 places 2,405 of 12,000 move, 20.0 percent, all to Saffron; at one place each, 721, all from Pewter. Back at eight horses and 128 places, give the sturdier horses twice the places: Juniper carries 2,487 of a fair 2,400. Last, at eight horses, try evenly spaced and add a horse (4,784 move), then mod at eight and add one (10,665).

explain.oneLine: No ghost rides Marigold. A rider is a pass record, and Marigold owns 169 of the ring's 360 degrees, so it holds 47 percent of the records. When Dapple went off, its whole arc, and every rider in it, passed to the next horse clockwise: Marigold.

steps.title: Each horse owns the arc behind it.
steps.text: The Cache in Every Zone, in Season 2, gave consistent hashing in a paragraph. A key is the value used to place a record, and a node is one server in the group. Placing works in three steps. Hash each node onto a ring of numbers, once, when it joins. Hash each key onto the same ring. Walk clockwise from the key to the first node: the key belongs there. Cressida's Carousel is exactly that, with passes for keys and horses for nodes. A hash scatters keys roughly evenly round the ring, so a node's share of keys is roughly its arc's share of the ring. Marigold's arc is 169 degrees, 47 percent of the ring, and it holds 5,645 of 12,000 passes, 47.0 percent. Pewter's is a hundredth of a degree and holds none. Hand-picked degrees did this here, but random ones aren't much better. Dynamo is the database Amazon built for its own shop, and its paper says the random position assignment of each node on the ring leads to non-uniform data and load distribution. In the sim, the same eight horses with one hashed place each still leave the busiest carrying 3.30 times its fair share.

steps.title: A horse that leaves hands everything to one neighbour.
steps.text: Removing a node moves only its keys, which is the ring's promise. It happens in steps. The node leaves the ring. Every key in its arc now walks clockwise past the gap. With one place per node, they all stop at the same place: the next node clockwise, which must now copy in and carry all of them. Dapple's 1,414 riders all landed on Marigold, which went from 5,645 to 7,059. If Marigold went off, all 5,645 would land on Juniper. Adding is the mirror image. Nutmeg, bolted at one hashed degree, takes the riders just behind it from one neighbour, Tansy, 691 of them, and every other horse is untouched. Dynamo's paper puts it as the departure or arrival of a node only affects its immediate neighbors. That is cheap in moves and bad for load, since one neighbour takes the whole shock.

steps.title: Many places per horse: virtual nodes.
steps.text: The fix is to give each physical node, each real machine, many positions on the ring, called virtual nodes or vnodes. Setting them up takes steps. Pick a count for each machine, more for bigger ones. Hash the machine's name with each number from 1 to that count, giving that many points. Put the machine on the ring at every one of those points. Keys then walk clockwise exactly as before. Dynamo: a virtual node looks like a single node in the system, but each node can be responsible for more than one. Each position is still a random arc, but a node's share is now the sum of many arcs, and sums of many random pieces land close to their average. In the sim, with 12,000 riders and eight horses, the busiest horse against its fair share falls from 3.76 with one place each to 1.77 with 4, 1.46 with 16, 1.23 with 32 and 1.06 with 128. It narrows roughly with the square root of the places: four times the places brings it about half as far above fair. And it is luck, not a law: 256 places came out at 1.09, a little worse than 128, because 12,000 riders scatter unevenly too. When a node leaves, its many small arcs pass to many different neighbours. At 128 places Dapple's 1,540 riders went to all seven horses, at most 278 to any one. And places can follow capacity, how much a machine can carry: in Dynamo's words, the number of virtual nodes that a node is responsible can decided based on its capacity. With 256 places for Juniper and Tansy, Juniper carries 2,487 against a fair 2,400.

steps.title: Adding a fifth node to four moves about a fifth of the keys.
steps.text: When a node joins a ring, it happens in steps. The new node takes its places on the ring. Each place cuts an arc that a neighbour owned in two. The keys in the new node's half are copied over from that neighbour, and from then on lookups for them stop at the new node. If lookups switch before the copy lands, those keys can't be found for a while. So the keys that move are exactly the ones the new node now owns. With n nodes before, a new node's fair share is 1 in n + 1, so adding a fifth node to four should move about a fifth. Measure it rather than trust it. In the sim, four horses with 128 places each become five: 2,405 of 12,000 riders move, 20.0 percent, all of them to the new horse, taken from all four old ones. With one place each the same addition moves 721, 6.0 percent, all from one neighbour, because one random arc is rarely a fair share. Dynamo says that with virtual nodes the newly available node accepts a roughly equivalent amount of load from each of the other available nodes. Seating by mod instead, the remainder after dividing by the number of nodes, would move 9,600 of the 12,000 for the same change, since most keys' remainders change. This is the measurement Gatekeeper's G4 Build Night asks for.

steps.title: Copies walk to the next different horses.
steps.text: Copies of a record are called replicas. With one place per node, the next place clockwise is always another node, so the old rule, put the copy on the next node, was safe. With many places, the next place often belongs to the same node. In the sim, with 128 places and the old walk, 1,285 riders have both of their 2 copies on one horse, and 3,571 have two of their 3 copies on one. A copy on the same machine is no copy: they fail together. Dynamo's rule fixes it, in steps. The coordinator, the node in charge of that key, starts at the key's place. It walks clockwise. At each place it asks which machine owns it, and skips it if that machine already holds a copy. It stops when it has enough different machines. Where N is the number of copies, in the paper's words, the coordinator replicates keys at the N-1 clockwise successor nodes, and the preference list is built by skipping positions in the ring to ensure that the list contains only distinct physical nodes. With skipping on, the sim's count is 0 for any number of copies. Real systems go one step further and spread copies over failure domains, groups of machines that can fail together. A rack, one cabinet of servers sharing power and network, is one; a datacenter, a building full of them, is another. Cassandra, a widely used free database, says in its docs that NetworkTopologyStrategy attempts to choose replicas within a datacenter from different racks, and each replica is guaranteed to be chosen from a different rack when there are at least as many racks as copies.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for the night after. The ring in the middle has 1,280 places: 128 for each horse and 256 for the sturdier Juniper and Tansy, and each rider's copies go to the next different horses clockwise. Riders against fair share: Marigold 1,219 of 1,200, Pewter 1,310 of 1,200, Dapple 1,353 of 1,200, Juniper 2,487 of 2,400, Saffron 1,031 of 1,200, Tansy 2,211 of 2,400, Cobweb 1,215 of 1,200, Clover 1,174 of 1,200. With Dapple off, its 1,353 riders scatter over all seven; Nutmeg joining takes 1,167.

notes.text: Dapple off: its 1,353 riders scatter over all 7. Nutmeg joining takes 1,167.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the night after. Every horse has 128 places on the ring, the sturdier Juniper and Tansy 256, and each rider's copies go to the next different horses clockwise. Every horse now carries close to its fair share, a horse off for repair scatters its riders over all the others, and a new horse takes a little from every horse.

fix.title: The fix: many places per horse, more for the sturdier ones, and copies on different horses
fix.text: Give every horse many places on the ring, each hashed from its name and a number: 128 here, 256 for Juniper and Tansy, which have twice the memory. Make the change on a quiet night and count it, because changing the places moves riders once: 10,351 for the 128 places, 1,944 more for the sturdier horses' extra ones. Change the copy rule at the same time: from a rider's place, walk clockwise and take the next horse that doesn't already hold a copy, until there are enough. Then, before Nutmeg joins, work out its share and check the log afterwards: it should take about 1,167 riders, a few from every horse. Keep the ride log, and alert when any horse runs far from its fair share.

limits: Virtual nodes even out how many keys each node holds, not how often each key is used. One pass read a thousand times a second still lands on one horse however many places it has. That is a hot key, one value carrying far more work than the rest, and the fixes from Hot Key, such as copying the key or splitting it, still apply.

More places cost something. Cassandra calls each place a token. Its docs say every token adds up to 2 x (RF - 1) neighbours on the ring, where RF, the replication factor, is how many copies each record has. They say the more tokens you have, the higher the probability of an outage, a time when some data can't be reached. And the number of repair operations grows: the regular jobs that compare copies and fix any that differ. That is why Cassandra 4.0 cut its default from 256 tokens to 16 and turned on an allocator, a helper that places them evenly instead of at random.

Random places only average the luck out. They don't remove it. With 128 places per horse the busiest still ran 6 percent over its share, and 256 places did slightly worse than 128. Measure the load per node and the keys moved on every change rather than trusting the arithmetic.

explain.seniorTake: Consistent hashing solves one problem, moving few keys when the nodes change, and leaves another, balance, to how you place the nodes. One random position per node gives arcs that differ wildly, a node that leaves dumps its whole arc on one neighbour, and a node that joins takes from one neighbour only. Virtual nodes fix balance with averaging. Each machine takes many positions, so its share is the sum of many arcs and comes close to fair. A leaver's keys scatter over everyone, a joiner takes a little from everyone, and a bigger machine simply takes more positions. Then walk replicas, the copies, to different physical machines, and across racks or zones, groups that can fail together. Otherwise the extra positions quietly put two copies on one box. Choose the count on purpose: more positions balance better but add neighbours and upkeep work, which is why Cassandra now ships 16 tokens with an allocator rather than 256 random ones. And measure: per-node load against its fair share, and the keys moved on every change.

realWorld.title: Karger and others, STOC 1997: where the name comes from
realWorld.text: The term consistent hashing comes from a 1997 paper by David Karger, Eric Lehman, Tom Leighton, Matthew Levine, Daniel Lewin and Rina Panigrahy, Consistent Hashing and Random Trees: Distributed Caching Protocols for Relieving Hot Spots on the World Wide Web, presented at STOC 1997, the 29th ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing, in El Paso, Texas. ACM is the Association for Computing Machinery, a body for computer scientists. Its problem was the one in this case at web scale: spreading requests over a changing set of cache servers, servers that keep quick copies, so that a change moves few of them.

realWorld.title: Dynamo, SOSP 2007: virtual nodes and the preference list
realWorld.text: Amazon's Dynamo paper (DeCandia and others, SOSP 2007, a computer systems conference) describes the database Amazon built for its own shop. It treats the output range of a hash function as a fixed circular space or ring. Each node in the system is assigned a random value within this space which represents its position on the ring, and a key's node is found by walking the ring clockwise to find the first node with a position larger than the item's position. It names two problems with that basic scheme: the random position assignment of each node on the ring leads to non-uniform data and load distribution, and the basic algorithm is oblivious to the heterogeneity in the performance of nodes. In plain words: the shares come out uneven, and the scheme ignores that some machines are bigger than others. Its answer is virtual nodes: a virtual node looks like a single node in the system, but each node can be responsible for more than one virtual node. It lists three gains. If a node becomes unavailable (due to failures or routine maintenance), the load handled by this node is evenly dispersed across the remaining available nodes. A node that comes back or is added accepts a roughly equivalent amount of load from each of the other available nodes. And the number of virtual nodes that a node is responsible can decided based on its capacity, accounting for heterogeneity in the physical infrastructure. For copies, where N is the number of copies and the coordinator is the node in charge of a key, the coordinator replicates these keys at the N-1 clockwise successor nodes in the ring; the list of nodes that is responsible for storing a particular key is called the preference list, built by skipping positions in the ring to ensure that the list contains only distinct physical nodes.

realWorld.title: Cassandra: tokens, vnodes and their price
realWorld.text: Cassandra is a widely used free database that spreads data over many machines. Its architecture docs say it maps every node to one or more tokens on a continuous hash ring and defines ownership by hashing a key onto the ring, so that consistent hashing only has to move a small fraction of the keys. Virtual nodes solve the problem by assigning multiple tokens in the token ring to each physical node. When a new node is added it accepts approximately equal amounts of data from other nodes in the ring, and when a node is decommissioned, it loses data roughly equally to other members of the ring. A token is a node's position on the ring, and decommissioned means removed on purpose. The same page lists the costs, where RF, the replication factor, is the number of copies: every token introduces up to 2 * (RF - 1) additional neighbors on the token ring, the more tokens you have, the higher the probability of an outage, the number of discrete repair operations the cluster must do also increases, and cluster-wide maintenance operations are often slowed. For copies it offers two placement rules. SimpleStrategy walks the tokens and checks whether the owning node has been added to the set of replicas, until replication_factor distinct nodes have been added, and NetworkTopologyStrategy attempts to choose replicas within a datacenter from different racks.

realWorld.title: num_tokens: 256, then 16
realWorld.text: cassandra.yaml is the settings file each Cassandra node reads when it starts. In it, num_tokens defines the number of tokens randomly assigned to this node on the ring, and the more tokens, relative to other nodes, the larger the proportion of data that this node will store. The reference page lists its default value as 16, and also says that if you leave this unspecified, Cassandra will use the default of 1 token for legacy compatibility: the shipped file sets 16, and a file with the line removed gets 1. Cassandra 4.0's upgrade notes (CASSANDRA-13701) say that to give a better out of the box experience, the default num_tokens value has been changed from 256 to 16, and allocate_tokens_for_local_replication_factor is also uncommented and set to 3, so tokens are allocated for even ownership rather than at random. Out of the box means as shipped, before anyone changes a setting. They warn that a new node joining with a different num_tokens than the rest of the datacenter will be responsible for a different amount of data. The production guide says using more than one token-range per node is referred to as virtual nodes, or vnodes, and that more tokens leads to sharing data with more peers, and results in decreased availability. Its table says one token gives the fewest peers but inflexible expansion, where the cluster must double in size to stay balanced; that using 8 vnodes distributes the workload between systems with a ~10% variance; and that 16 is not recommended for clusters over 50 nodes. Those figures assume the token allocator, not random tokens like the sim's.

realWorld.title: Netflix EVCache: Ketama on the cache ring
realWorld.text: The Cache in Every Zone's 2013 Netflix post says the data in each EVCache cluster is sharded across the memcached nodes based on Ketama consistent hashing algorithm. EVCache is Netflix's cache, its store of quick copies; memcached is the program each cache server runs; and sharded means split. Ketama is the same idea as this case: each server is hashed to many points on the ring, so the keys of a server that fails spread over the rest.

asked: Explain consistent hashing. Why do you need virtual nodes?
You have four nodes and add a fifth. How many keys move?
How do you place replicas on a hash ring?
interview.answer: Hash every key and every node onto the same ring of numbers, and give each key to the next node clockwise. A key is the value that places a record; a node is one server. Compared with key mod number of nodes, where changing the count moves almost every key, a change on the ring moves only the keys between the changed node and its neighbour: a new node takes exactly the keys in its new arcs. With one random position per node, though, the arcs differ wildly, so some nodes hold several times their share, a node that leaves hands its whole arc to one neighbour, and a node that joins takes from one neighbour only. Virtual nodes fix that: each physical node takes many positions, its share becomes the sum of many arcs and lands close to fair, a leaver's keys scatter over all the others, and a bigger machine can take more positions. In my measurement, eight nodes and 12,000 keys went from 3.76 times a fair share with one position each to 1.06 with 128. Adding a fifth node to four should move about a fifth of the keys, all to the new node and a little from each old one; with 128 positions I measured 2,405 of 12,000, 20 percent, and I'd put that in a test. For replicas, the copies, walk clockwise from the key and take the next N different physical nodes, skipping positions that belong to a node you already chose. That is Dynamo's preference list; otherwise two copies can land on one machine. In production, the live system, also spread them across racks or zones, groups of machines that can fail together, like Cassandra's NetworkTopologyStrategy. Finally, mention the price: more positions mean more neighbours and more repair work, the jobs that compare copies and fix differences. That is why Cassandra moved its default from 256 tokens to 16 with an allocator.

terms.def: Rides and stalls on a seaside pier. Gullsway Pier's shuts from November to Easter, though its ice rink stays open.
A merry-go-round: wooden horses on a round platform that turns. Gullsway's has eight horses and holds 64 riders.
A ticket that lets one person in all season. Gullsway has 12,000, and the rink's gates check each one.
The office beside Gullsway's carousel where the season passes are kept and renewal letters are printed.
Cressida's 2011 system that keeps Gullsway's season passes on eight small servers, named after the horses, placed on a hash ring.
One of the Carousel's servers, a node on the ring, named after a wooden horse.
One season pass record. Its pass number is hashed to a point on the ring, and it lives on the horse that owns that point.
The Carousel's report at 03:00 each night: how many riders each horse carries.
The stretch of the ring a node owns: from the node before it, clockwise, up to its own position. Every key hashed into it belongs to that node.
The direction of rising numbers round the ring, like a clock's hands. A key goes to the first node position at or after its own, wrapping past the top back to zero.
One position a horse holds on the ring. As built, each horse has one; the fix gives each many.
One of many positions one real machine takes on the ring, like one person holding several raffle tickets. Its share is the sum of all its arcs. Also called a vnode.
The real machine behind one or more virtual nodes. Copies of a key must sit on different physical nodes.
The keys a node would hold if load matched capacity: the total divided by the nodes, with a node that has twice the places counted twice.
The sim's spread: the worst horse's riders divided by its fair share. 1.00 is perfect; 3.76 means nearly four times its share.
How many virtual nodes a machine gets compared with the others, set by its capacity. Juniper and Tansy have twice the places.
A second copy of a record kept on another server so one failure doesn't lose it, like a replica. The Carousel keeps one per rider.
Riders that sit on a different horse after a change than before it. Each one's record has to be copied to its new horse.
Placing nodes at equal distances round the ring by hand, such as every 45 degrees for eight. Even until the count changes.
A sim button that gives every horse new places drawn from the sim's seeded random numbers.
A group of machines that can fail together, such as one rack, one power feed or one availability zone.
A tall cabinet of servers in a datacenter that share power and network boxes, so they can fail together.
In Cassandra, a node's position on the hash ring. A node with several tokens has several virtual nodes.
Cassandra's setting for how many tokens, or vnodes, a node takes on the ring. The shipped cassandra.yaml has set 16 since version 4.0; before, 256.
Cassandra's main configuration file, read by each node when it starts.
A cassandra.yaml setting that has Cassandra choose a new node's ring positions so every node owns an even share, given how many copies each record has. Set to 3 by default since 4.0.
Cassandra's helper that chooses a new node's ring positions so shares come out even, like a seating plan instead of sitting anywhere.
A Cassandra rule for placing copies: walk the ring from the key's position, and add each node not already chosen, until there are as many as the number of copies wanted.
A Cassandra rule for placing copies: you set how many go in each datacenter, a building of servers, and it tries to put each copy in a different rack.
A regular upkeep job that compares the copies of each record and fixes any that differ. More tokens per node mean more separate repair jobs.
Removing a node from a cluster on purpose, handing its data to the others first.
The other nodes a node shares data with as neighbours on the ring. More tokens mean more peers.
Machines in one cluster being different: some bigger or faster than others. Dynamo gives bigger ones more virtual nodes.
The ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing, a yearly computer science conference. Consistent hashing was presented at the 1997 one.
The ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles, a computer systems conference. Dynamo was presented at the 2007 one.
The number that times itself gives another: the square root of 16 is 4. Quadrupling the places roughly halves how far the busiest sits above its share.
A rule in ISO/IEC 27001:2022, a security standard companies are checked against: watch how much of your machines you use, and adjust before you run out of room.

atWork: Picture a common incident. A team runs a cache, a store of quick copies, on four nodes. The program that talks to it places keys with consistent hashing, one position per node. One node runs at twice the others' memory and CPU, its processor, for months, and everyone blames its traffic. When they add a fifth node to relieve it, the new node takes keys from one neighbour and the hot node doesn't change at all. Look for the same in your own systems. Find what places keys on nodes: a client library's hashing (shared code the app calls), a cache cluster's own placement, Cassandra's num_tokens in cassandra.yaml, or a homegrown shard map, a hand-made list of which server holds what. Find out how many positions each node has and whether bigger machines get more. Then measure, with read-only access, which can look but not change anything. Count keys per node, divide by each node's fair share, and look at the worst. Copy a sample of real keys and replay an addition offline, on a test machine: how many keys would move, and from which nodes? And check the replica walk, how copies are placed: does it skip a node that already holds a copy, and does it spread copies across racks or zones? This rehearses the G4 Build Night in Gatekeeper. Build a consistent-hashing balancer, a program that spreads requests over servers, with a setting for the number of virtual nodes. Write the test that adds a fifth backend server to four and checks that roughly a fifth of keys move, within a margin you can justify. Record in docs/decisions.md how many virtual nodes you chose and why. It also feeds Loadout's L4 data tier, where placement uses consistent hashing. If your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, a security standard, control A.8.6 (capacity management) expects resource use to be monitored and adjusted against current and expected capacity needs. A load measure per node, with an alert when one drifts from its fair share, is the kind of evidence that supports it. If it is pursuing a SOC 2 report, an outside check of a company's controls, that includes the availability category, criterion A1.1 expects the entity to maintain, monitor and evaluate current processing capacity. So build the measurement in now rather than at audit time.

recall.prompt: A team's cache, a store of quick copies, runs on four nodes. The app places keys on them with consistent hashing, one position per node on the ring. One node holds 41 percent of the keys and runs hot. Last month they added a fifth node to relieve it, and the new node took keys from only one of the four, not the hot one. What is going on, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: One random position per node gives arcs of very different sizes, so a node's share of keys follows its arc; and a new node takes keys only from the one neighbour after it
Give every node many virtual nodes (positions) on the ring, weighted by capacity, so shares average out close to fair
Then adding a fifth node to four moves about a fifth of the keys, a little from every node; measure it

recall.model: One position per node gives arcs of very different sizes, and a node holds the keys in its arc. So one node can own 41 percent of the ring while another owns a sliver. A new node with one position lands in a single arc and takes keys only from one neighbour, the node just after it, which here wasn't the hot one. Give every node many virtual nodes, a hundred or more positions each, weighted by capacity so bigger machines take more. Each node's share is then the sum of many arcs and lands close to fair. A node that leaves scatters its keys over all the others, and adding a fifth node to four moves about a fifth of the keys, a little from every node. Measure it: count keys per node against fair share, and the keys moved on the change.

recall.prompt: Four nodes with 128 virtual nodes each hold 12,000 keys on a hash ring. You add a fifth node with 128. About how many keys move, and where?
options: About 2,400, all of them to the new node, a little from each old one
About 3,000, spread over all five nodes
About 9,600, because the number of nodes changed
None until someone runs a rebalance
recall.why: A new node takes exactly the keys in its new arcs, and with many positions its share is close to fair: one fifth of 12,000 is 2,400. In the sim it was 2,405, 20.0 percent, all to the new node, from all four old ones. About 9,600 is what key mod number of nodes moves for the same change.

recall.prompt: Your team moves a six-node store from one ring position per node to 64 positions each. Replication factor, the number of copies of each key, stays 3, and the code still puts a key's copies on the next 3 positions clockwise. A week later one machine dies and some keys can't be read at all. Why, and what should the replica code do?

keyIdeas.idea: With many positions, the next positions clockwise often belong to the same machine, so several copies of a key sit on one machine and die with it
Walk clockwise but skip positions whose machine already holds a copy, until there are N distinct physical nodes (Dynamo's preference list)
Also spread the copies over failure domains such as racks or zones

recall.model: With 64 positions per machine, the next positions clockwise often belong to the same machine, so some keys had two or all three copies on one physical node, and when it died those keys went with it. Change the walk: go clockwise from the key, and skip any position whose machine already holds a copy, until you have 3 distinct physical nodes. That is Dynamo's preference list, built by skipping positions so it holds only distinct physical nodes. Then go one step further and spread the copies across racks or availability zones, as Cassandra's NetworkTopologyStrategy tries to, so one failure domain can't take every copy.

recall.prompt: In Dynamo, a machine with twice the capacity of the others is given twice as many virtual nodes. What does that do?
options: Every key gets two copies on it, so it serves reads twice as fast
It answers each request in half the time
It owns about twice as much of the ring, so it holds about twice the keys
It becomes the coordinator for every key
recall.why: Each virtual node owns an arc, and a machine's share is the sum of its arcs, so twice the positions gives about twice the share. Dynamo says the number of virtual nodes a node is responsible for can be decided by its capacity, accounting for heterogeneity. Copies are a separate rule: they must sit on distinct physical nodes.

recall.prompt: Cassandra 4.0 changed the num_tokens in its shipped cassandra.yaml. From what, to what, and why?
options: From 1 to 256, so data spreads more evenly
From 256 to 16, with a token allocator turned on, since more tokens mean more peers and lower availability
From 16 to 256, so new nodes take load from everyone
From 256 to 1, to make repairs faster
recall.why: The 4.0 notes (CASSANDRA-13701) say the default changed from 256 to 16 for a better out of the box experience, with allocate_tokens_for_local_replication_factor set to 3 so tokens are placed for even ownership. The docs explain the trade-off: more tokens means sharing data with more peers and decreased availability, and more repair operations.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 7 months later. The Carousel has run on 128 places per horse since January, 256 for Juniper and Tansy, and the ride log has stayed flat. In October Cressida added a tenth horse, Quince, on a new server, ready for the Christmas market. Its config file, the settings it reads at start-up, came from the server's installer, not from the other horses. The next morning's ride log shows every horse carrying over a thousand riders and Quince carrying a handful. Cressida says that's fine: "it'll fill up as people buy passes".
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What's going on, and what should Cressida do?

keyIdeas.idea: Quince has far fewer places than the others, likely the installer's default, so it owns a sliver of the ring and won't fill up: new passes land by hash, at the same small share
Give Quince the same number of places as the others (or in proportion to its capacity), and expect it to take about its fair share, a little from every horse
Measure: check the riders per horse and the riders moved after the fix, and alert when a horse drifts far from its fair share; copy settings from the other horses, not an installer

coldCase.model: Quince almost certainly has the installer's default number of places, probably one, while every other horse has 128 or 256. A horse's share is the sum of its arcs, so one place among about 1,280 owns a sliver of the ring. It won't fill up: new passes are hashed to the ring like old ones and land on Quince at the same small share. Cassandra's 4.0 notes warn about exactly this, a new node with a different num_tokens being responsible for a different amount of data. Give Quince 128 places, the same as the others, or more if its server is bigger, and do it on a quiet night: it should then take about its fair share, a little from every horse. Measure it: count riders per horse and riders moved, and add an alert when any horse runs far from its fair share. And copy new horses' config from the running ones, not from an installer.
